title: The day that I decided to stop using Windows
text:
Introduction
During my undergraduate studies, my professor Paulo Justiniano always incentivized the students for using any Linux distribution on their machines. The reasons were vast, but I will give the details later on.
I never tried it before because:

I was comfortable using Windows because I used this operational system on my internship and at home
I did not have a personal laptop at the beginning of university.

On my last year of college, I bought one with Windows pre installed, and I was using as it is (knowing that migrating to Ubuntu would be better). But the day came!

title: The day that I decided to stop using Windows
text:
The Day
I remember like it was today. It was during the time that everyone was migrating from Windows 8.1 or 10. I was working on a report, had worked the full day on it, and then I decided to migrate to Windows 10. The migration finished successfully, I opened the file, started typing a few more words, and then, out of nothing my report became corrupted:







I could not save or send my report to anywhere, and I received the famous blue screen:







I had to turn off and on my PC using the power button, but I could not see the original content of the file anymore. It was gone. At the same time, I downloaded the Mint iso file, burn into a Pen Drive, installed it and started using.
It was not only flowers at the beginning, as usual. My friend Augusto Colombo helped my in the lab to install and do the basics. Some weeks later, and I did not like the Mint, so I swap to Ubuntu.

title: The day that I decided to stop using Windows
text:
The redemption



With Ubuntu everything fell into place. All the troubles that I had when tried a fresh install on Mint it was solved on Ubuntu, and I could fix by my self.
It really represents the meaning of Ubuntu, from African: “I am what I am because of who we all are”. Ever since then I use ubuntu on my personal laptop and in my current job. It is so amazing.
It gives many advantages for me compared to the time I had Windows:

I know how to do a fresh install when needed.
It is free to use. Don’t need to pay any license.
It hardly enters a virus.
The performance does not go down over time.
There is a full community open to help.
Due to the fact that most of installation is made via CLI, it opens your mind to shell, to automate your repetitive tasks.
The hard drive is portable. I can remove from my PC and plug it into another. It will not crash.

When we talk specifically about Data Science tasks, I can list:

Python is pre-installed on Ubuntu.
Docker only runs on Ubuntu machines.
Almost every server in the world uses a distro based on Linux. Choosing a server on EC2, it is like to choose which Linux you want to use. Using Ubuntu daily means that when I need to access servers, I am more familiar with the operational system.
Installation of tools for data science such as R, Python, dependencies are usually easily handed on Ubuntu.
A common task on a DS work is to tell the path you files are. If you are on Windows, you need to copy the path, paste on a Editor and make the back slash into forward the slash, or double it. With Ubuntu, you do not. You use as it is.

The only thing that sometimes I miss on Ubuntu is the Office package. But using Libre Office is lighter, free and it is a good alternative full of customizations.

title: The day that I decided to stop using Windows
text:
Considerations
I am aware that the latest Windows release have become better, such that, WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) became available and Windows 10 is stable now. From another point of view, Ubuntu has now Steam for gaming, but it is still not ideal when you want a full gaming experience. In the end of the day, it is always a matter of which operational system suits you best: just like for designers that love Apple.
With all that given, it would be nice if we could choose the operational system that fits better our role, instead of going to the usual operational system.
Maybe we can reach a day that:



Leave in the comments any thoughts about it!
Happy coding!

title: Ruff in a Nutshell + Configuring it on VsCode
text:
Hello guys!
Today I want to talk about RUFF, my default formatter (and much more) for Python language.
In a nutshell, RUFF can be seen as a tool that performs all these tasks:
RUFF = Flake8 + isort + black + pydocstyle + pyupgrade + autoflake
Flake8 = Linter, which fix style + syntax errors
isort = Sort the imports
black = formatter ; PEP8 complaint. Ex.: line-length: 88; Single/Double quotes; empty lines; parenthesis
pydocstyle = docstrings
pyupgrade = upgrade syntax for newer versions of python packages
autoflake = Remove unused imports and unused variables
So, instead of having to set up each one individually, use RUFF and have all these tools into a single one. RUFF was written in rust, so it is not a wrap of the previously mentioned. Also, it is way faster than the previous tools.

title: Ruff in a Nutshell + Configuring it on VsCode
Ruff in a Nutshell + Configuring it on VsCode
text:
Bonus (Caveat)
I struggled to start using a tool like this because I used to write code in a single long line. I always received the E501: line-too-long warning from black. It happens when the number of characters in a line is longer than 79 characters, which is the recommendation in PEP 8. After applying a tool like ruff my code changed drastically (as it would force me to break lines), and it was uncomfortable in the beginning. So, I started to relax the parameter of the line-length a little bit (from 79 to for example, 150 characters) and started to analyze the impact of change. Then I realized that the impact on my previous code was not large at all.
Leaving the limit as the default, PEP 8 argues that you can open multiple files side by side, making also easier to see the git diff changes.
Anyway, if you think that this limit is small, you can relax it a little bit globally, doing it by:
[tool.ruff]
line-length = 130

lint.ignore = [
    "E501", # Ignore long lines
    "E302", # Ignore blank lines issue
    "E701", # Ignore single-line if statements
]
extend-include = ["*.ipynb"]

[tool.ruff.format]
quote-style = "double"
docstring-code-format = true

[tool.ruff.lint.pydocstyle] # It enforces that all functions have docstrings
convention = "google"
or skipping this rule by adding # fmt: skip at the end of a line. Or use #fmt: on at the beginning of a block and #fmt: off at the end.
Happy coding.

title: MAPE and its pitfalls
text: Hello guys! I want to talk a widely used metric, specially in time series modelling, which it is MAPE.

title: MAPE and its pitfalls
text:
Why MAPE is used
MAPE is a largely used metric because has the following benefits:

It is a percentage metric; so, it can be used to compare time series with different units.
It is largely used. People specially from other fields use it without knowing that are using it because it is so straight forward and natural.

I will give an example for the last bit: Let’s suppose that a salesperson had to sell 100 pairs of boots, but he sold 80, so how far is he from the target? Well, (80-100)/100 = -0,20 = -20%. So the salesperson is 20% far from the target. The formula for MAPE can be described as:
\[\text{MAPE} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left| \frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{y_i} \right|}{n}\]
which is so intuitive. However, behind this popularity, MAPE has several pitfalls, specially when working with high number of time series at the same time:

title: MAPE and its pitfalls
text:
MAPE is a biased metric:
To give a simple example, let’s suppose that our ypred is 100; if the yreal is 150, we have a MAPE equals to 0.33, in contrast to MAPE equals 1 if yreal is 50. So, MAPE will always push toward to biased underforecasting.
The following table illustrate this:

title: MAPE and its pitfalls
section: MAPE is not define when y_true is zero
text:
MAPE is not define when y_true is zero
The denominator of mape is y_true. So, MAPE might return NaN on your programming software or Inf. In order to “fix” it, what many people do is to set y_true to a small value near to zero, which is what sklearn.metrics.mean_average_percentage_error do (setting y_true to \(2.22x10^-16\)). But it gives other problems: 1. Setting y_true to \(2.22x10^-16\) will lead to a even higher MAPE number; 2. You will never know a “true” value of the error for this series; 3. Your prediction will be compromised even if your predictions are really good (let’s say 0.00001); 4. If you need to aggregate the metric of this series with other series, your comparison will be compromised because the resulting MAPE will be towards a very high number.
In practical terms, see how MAPE will behave if for a true value of 0, we set 9E-17 for the last two rows of the table:

title: MAPE and its pitfalls
section: MAPE does not minimizes the error towards the mean value
text:
MAPE does not minimizes the error towards the mean value
This is not a pitfall, but it is a warning, because usually people want to be right on average, and this is not what MAPE does. In contrast, it will give a prediction towards a biased median, if I can so.
A very good resource to read about is shortcomings of MAPE, that will lead to many other resources.

title: Sofle v2 keyboard is cheaper than a wrist exam
text:
Introduction
I am one of those programmers who type at list 8 hours per day and still prefer shopping on a PC rather than on a phone rsrs. Yes, I need the big screens.
Even tough I did not count my words per minute (wpm), I considered myself a good typist with my 100% keyboard: I was able to memorize the shortcuts that I needed and did not have to look on the keyboard to type.

When the pain started
But as time goes by, I started to feel that my hands started to get rust, like some oil was missing between my hand bones 🤖. Three years later, I paid US$ 100 in an ultrasound that showed me that I had tendonitis 🤕. I started to the physiotherapy for my wrist, which gave me some relief, but at the end of day, I felt sour on my right hand due to labour.


Looking for a new keyboard
So, I started to look for a new keyboard. I was willing to buy a simple used mechanical keyboard; it would be a lot better than my membrane keyboard. But the pain would still remain. Then, I decided to buy an Ajazz Alice AKS068 Pro from a Brazilian Fellow online:








The price was great.
The change would be small because it is a 70% keyboard.
I loved the colors.
There was a Knob button that I would use as a volume controller.
It was “ergonomic”.




HOWEVER, he did not want to send the keyboard over mail.



Then, I found pricy this keyboard new, here is way:

The keyboard was not ergonomic at all -> It only had curved keys in a fixed position;
As time passed by, the pain increased, and I felt that I need something more complete;

title: Sofle v2 keyboard is cheaper than a wrist exam
text:
Mechanical ergonomic keyboards
A week or later I discovered the Moonlander keyboard from Fabio Akita, for US$ 400, no way. But I realized that this was the kind of technology that I needed. So I did a vast research and I found out that eFeXx built a Sofle v2 keyboard by himself step by step. There was even a ready to go shop list. With this keyboard I would have a real ergonomic keyboard, that’s way:

The keys are columns oriented: They respect the different length of the fingers.
The thumb finger receives 3 keys to use on each split. Being it the strongest finger is a waste to use only for space in a regular keyboard.
I could place the keyboard at any angle that I wanted: as long as I respect the ergonomics.
The splits can be placed far apart from which other.

It also has two knobs (one for volume and another for page up/down), two screens, and can be powered with leds, bluetooth and much more from the creator. But it was not still perfect, here is way: the case for the keyboard on the video did not work and had to used a flat one.

title: Sofle v2 keyboard is cheaper than a wrist exam
text:
Building my own keyboard
That’s when my friend Seiji enters into the history. I got so excited about building my own keyboard, that I not only convinced him to make one for himself, but he also developed an angled support case based on this one, with a better support for the PCB. This was the Gran Finale of ergonomics manual.
Then, the next step was to buy all the parts from AliExpress, one by one, and assemble them together:

 

This whole process took me 1 full Saturday and other 3 months of “CI/CD” that I had to fix some welds. Considering that I had no previous experience on weld, it was a learning process, and I liked.

title: Sofle v2 keyboard is cheaper than a wrist exam
text:
In summary
This is what I got from this process:

I made a new friendship! Not only one, two: Paludo showed me his lilly keyboard and all the advantages of having a split keyboard.
Learned how to (and not to) weld.
I recommend it, specially if you are familiar with weld;
Like when we are new to programming, when I finished, I figured out that there was a better way to make it. I could have saved a lot money and time if I had bought a ready to build sofle RGB mx kit2 by 50 US$. But as part of my learning, I could not know that it would work before doing it.
Lots of stories for a Sunday in family.
A Blog post 😂;

This whole process made me remember that, to be a master, you gotta get your hands dirty!
Now, better coding, with better keyboards!!

title: How I made LGBM to work in GPU inside Docker and decrease image size by 70%
text:
First things first
In my daily routine as a data scientist at [4kst startup](https://4kst.ai/), I create the following demand for myself: “I need to make the LGBM model to run using GPU inside the container because it is broken in production. So far, so good. However, instead of”only fixing it”, I decided to approach it holistically. This was my current Dockerfile:
FROM nvidia/cuda:12.6.3-runtime-ubuntu24.04
# INSTALL CONDA

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y wget
RUN wget https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-py39_24.11.1-0-Linux-x86_64.sh
RUN bash Miniconda3-py39_24.11.1-0-Linux-x86_64.sh -b -p /opt/conda
ENV PATH="/opt/conda/bin:${PATH}"

# CREATE PIPELINE CONDA ENV

WORKDIR /usr/src/pipeline
COPY ./gpu-time-series-env.yaml .
RUN conda env create -f gpu-time-series-env.yaml
ENV CONDA_OVERRIDE_CUDA=12.2

SHELL ["conda", "run", "-n", "gpu_time_series", "/bin/bash", "-c"]

RUN conda install -c conda-forge tensorflow-gpu=2.17.0 lightgbm=4.6.0
RUN conda install conda-forge::flash-attn-layer-norm==2.6.3
RUN pip install xgboost==3.0.5

# COPY CODE AND RUN

COPY . .
CMD [ \
    "bash", "-c", \
    "source /opt/conda/etc/profile.d/conda.sh && \
    conda activate gpu_time_series && \
    conda config --set channel_priority strict && \
    python3 main.docker.py" \
]

title: How I made LGBM to work in GPU inside Docker and decrease image size by 70%
How I made LGBM to work in GPU inside Docker and decrease image size by 70%
text:
How everything got solved:

LightGBM

First of all, I put it back all packages inside the conda, because I wanted to use conda the single source of truth, and it would guarantee that its solver would not break in the Dockerfile.
Then, I realized that lightgbm installs two libraries:

liblightgbm which is the C++ code;
lightgbm which is the Python API.


Since one of them was installed by conda-forge channel, and another by defaults., it created a version mismatch between then, which did not make possible to use the GPU inside the container. Therefore, I reinstalled them using only conda-forge, which is the recommended channel nowadays.

⚠️ GOOD PRACTICE ALERT: Use only a single channel when creating a conda env.

In addition to that, conda-forge itself has three different ways to install its package: cuda, gpu or cpu. It also needs to be specified in the yaml. In this case, I did liblightgbm=4.6.0=cuda* and lightgbm=4.6.0=cuda*. cuda because is more modern than gpu. It guarantees that conda-forge would pick a cuda version of this library. I could be even more restrict to enforce cuda to be a specific version, but I set it loose.


flash-attn
It was also a bit pain, because it needs to be installed after pytorch (that’s way it was out of the conda env) once I installed from pip, which has an import pytorch after installation.

The good news is that after installing from conda-forge, this pre-installation process does not exists, and made possible to include it inside the conda env, with no ordering needed.



Cuda versions
What I realized is that inside the (gpu-time-series-env.yaml), I already had cuda (cuda-version=12.9). Therefore, it allowed me to get rid of image that install cuda and the CONDA_OVERRIDE_CUDA env var. Letting conda be the only one responsible by solving cuda.
It could be a good solution, but it would not last long because my cuda environment was created using conda env export --no-builds, which only describes the environment, i.e. it lists the packages that I want. But it does not specify the builds, because these builds are from the respective machine where I am using, and may not be compatible inside the machine I need to install it (I had problem with it before installing using only conda env export).
To solve this, I used conda-lock, which is a package that locks the exact dependency resolution needed to reproduce an environment. It solves conda versioning of the packages and save it with all information needed to a fresh install.

title: How I made LGBM to work in GPU inside Docker and decrease image size by 70%
text:
Channels strict and conda lock
Once all packages are from conda-forge:

I no longer need conda config --set channel_priority strict
I no longer need miniconda (which has default and conda-forge channels available):

I switched to miniforge which is the miniconda of only conda-forge channel, being lightweight.

title: How I made LGBM to work in GPU inside Docker and decrease image size by 70%
text:
Optimized Dockerfile
After applying all theses changes, I was able to come up with the following solution:
FROM ubuntu:24.04

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y wget && \
    wget https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh -O /tmp/miniforge.sh && \
    bash /tmp/miniforge.sh -b -p /opt/conda && rm /tmp/miniforge.sh

ENV PATH="/opt/conda/bin:${PATH}"

# CREATE PIPELINE CONDA ENV
WORKDIR /usr/src/pipeline

COPY conda-lock.yml .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir conda-lock && \
    conda-lock install --micromamba --name gpu_time_series conda-lock.yml && \
    pip uninstall -y conda-lock && \
    conda clean -afy && \
    rm -rf /opt/conda/pkgs/cache/* ~/.cache/pip ~/.cache/conda-lock ~/.mamba ~/.local/share/mamba

# Activate environment for RUN commands
SHELL ["conda", "run", "-n", "gpu_time_series", "/bin/bash", "-c"]

COPY . .

CMD [ \
    "bash", "-c", \
    "source /opt/conda/etc/profile.d/conda.sh && \
    conda activate gpu_time_series && \
    python3 main.docker.py" \
    ]
Which is 20% faster to build and a 70% lighter image than the previous Dockerfile because:

Ubuntu and miniforge are lighter;
I have used micromamba as well cleared all cache from package installation;
Started using .dockerignore.

title: How I made LGBM to work in GPU inside Docker and decrease image size by 70%
text:
Next Steps
I want to separate the gpu-time-series-env.yaml file into development and production, so I can save even more space on disk!
Happy coding!

title: How I made LGBM to work in GPU inside Docker and decrease image size by 70%
text:
Some Concepts
Containers are a way to encapsulate your application and dependencies that can be installed in a different machine without the need to install every instruction manually. Unlike Virtual Machines (VMs), it does not virtualize the hardware, neither operates in a new Operational System (OS). Instead, it shares the same kernel of the host machine, with no overhead when it is operating inside a linux (that’s also way I use Ubuntu), or a little overhead with Windows (it needs to be use WSL and Hypervision) or MacOS.
In Data Science, we need a lighter, fast and isolated piece of software, that’s way containers are handy. We do not need to have another entire system to our disposal.
When we run FROM: ubuntu:24.04 in Dockerfile we are not installing a fresh new Ubuntu for that container. We are only installing some parts of the Ubuntu, such as bash, apt and /usr, /etc folders, while having the same kernel of the host (it is not even necessary to have the same version of the linux, as long as the kernel supports it).
Lastly, but not least, Docker is a tool that manages the containers :). Dockerfile is the filename used to create an image, that containers can be created from it.

title: Is Python a Statically or Dynamically Typed Language?
text:
Today, I am going to talk about the characteristics of Python.
These are very common topics addressed in Python interviews. It allows the interviewer to know if the candidate knows the foundation of the language.
Have you ever received a TypeError while running your Python program?
It occurs because Python is a dynamic type language. It means the language verifies variable types during execution (runtime) - not during compilation, even though Python does compile your code into bytecode before running it. The type check only happens the instant an operation is actually executed, not when the code is first parsed and compiled.
Let’s go with an example:
def python_dynamic_language_example(execute_invalid_operation):
    print("The function was compiled to bytecode already")

    if execute_invalid_operation:
        a = 5
        b = "5"
        return a + b
    return "No invalid operation was found"
This function can run successfully even though there is an invalid operation inside the if clause:
python_dynamic_language_example(False)

The function was compiled to bytecode already


'No invalid operation was found'
Moreover, since this is a Quarto document, the mere fact that the whole .qmd file compiled successfully already shows the function was compiled to bytecode without error.
However, when we try to access the code portion that does the calculation, we receive the TypeError:
python_dynamic_language_example(True)

The function was compiled to bytecode already



---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[3], line 1
----> 1 python_dynamic_language_example(True)

Cell In[1], line 7, in python_dynamic_language_example(execute_invalid_operation)
      3 
      4     if execute_invalid_operation:
      5         a = 5
      6         b = "5"
----> 7         return a + b
      8     return "No invalid operation was found"

TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
which means that Python did not perform the operation because it was operated between two invalid types, even though it was compiled, as can be seen by dis:
import dis
dis.dis(python_dynamic_language_example)

  1           0 RESUME                   0

  2           2 LOAD_GLOBAL              1 (NULL + print)
             12 LOAD_CONST               1 ('The function was compiled to bytecode already')
             14 CALL                     1
             22 POP_TOP

  4          24 LOAD_FAST                0 (execute_invalid_operation)
             26 POP_JUMP_IF_FALSE        9 (to 46)

  5          28 LOAD_CONST               2 (5)
             30 STORE_FAST               1 (a)

  6          32 LOAD_CONST               3 ('5')
             34 STORE_FAST               2 (b)

  7          36 LOAD_FAST                1 (a)
             38 LOAD_FAST                2 (b)
             40 BINARY_OP                0 (+)
             44 RETURN_VALUE

  8     >>   46 RETURN_CONST             4 ('No invalid operation was found')
The fact that Python compiled this code, it means that it is dynamically type, instead of statically typed:
The fact that Python did not allow that operation occur in runtime means that it is strongly typed, instead of weakly typed:
Having these concepts in mind can help you to think on which language to use, or anticipate errors.

title: Is Python a Statically or Dynamically Typed Language?
text:
Flexibility in Python
Even though this is an odd behavior in Python, it allows you the change the variable type while programming:

a = 5
print(type(a))
print(id(a))
a = "5"
print(type(a))
print(id(a))

<class 'int'>
94417963138472
<class 'str'>
94417963199496


It occurs because the value has a type (dynamic type language), not the variable. It also allows you to write less boilerplate code, and make your code into production faster.

title: Is Python a Statically or Dynamically Typed Language?
section: What if you want to put more restrictions in Python ?
text:
What if you want to put more restrictions in Python ?
In recent Python versions (3.x), what you can do is add type annotation to variables and output of functions. However, it will still allow the function to be compiled:

def python_dynamic_language_example_typed(
    execute_invalid_operation: bool,
) -> str | TypeError:
    print("The function was compiled to bytecode already")

    if execute_invalid_operation:
        a: int = 5
        b: str = "5"
        return a + b
    return "No invalid"

dis.dis(python_dynamic_language_example_typed)

  1           0 RESUME                   0

  4           2 LOAD_GLOBAL              1 (NULL + print)
             12 LOAD_CONST               1 ('The function was compiled to bytecode already')
             14 CALL                     1
             22 POP_TOP

  6          24 LOAD_FAST                0 (execute_invalid_operation)
             26 POP_JUMP_IF_FALSE        9 (to 46)

  7          28 LOAD_CONST               2 (5)
             30 STORE_FAST               1 (a)

  8          32 LOAD_CONST               3 ('5')
             34 STORE_FAST               2 (b)

  9          36 LOAD_FAST                1 (a)
